canberra.title: Sandy Bigna’s poetic children’s story of overcoming grief claims ACT’s Book of the Year
canberra.snippet: Author Sandy Bigna’s young adult fiction book, Little Bones, has been named the 2026 ACT Book of the Year, pipping seven other shor...
canberra.content:
Canberra author Sandy Bigna’s children’s novel Little Bones has been named the 2026 ACT Book of the Year. Photo: Sandy Bigna.

Author Sandy Bigna’s young adult fiction book, Little Bones, has been named the 2026 ACT Book of the Year, pipping seven other shortlisted novels for the honour.

Ms Bigna’s 256-page novel follows an 11-year-old named Bones, who is grieving the death of her brother a year earlier.

One night, Bones unintentionally wishes upon a full moon for a bird to be resurrected, and both Bones and the bird, known as Bird, form a close friendship.

However, when Bird asks for the wish to be undone, Bones grapples with the challenges of losing another friend/family member.

ACT judges said the book stood out for its tender, poetic and assured storytelling, while also praising it as a profound meditation on grief, friendship and healing that leaves a lasting emotional impression on readers.

As a born-and-bred Canberran, Ms Bigna said it was an honour to be shortlisted alongside other renowned authors, including Merlinda Bobis and Martin Thomas.

“To be announced the winner absolutely blew me away,” she said.

“I find myself sort of always leaning towards having Canberra as a setting for most of the stories I write. So to win an award which celebrates Canberra-based authors, I think, is especially meaningful, and the judge’s comments were so lovely.”

Ms Bigna said she wrote the book in verse to create a personal, emotional connection between the characters and readers.

She explained that the rhythmic storytelling style let her naturally explore the themes of grief and loss at the centre of the story.

“I have always loved poetry, and I grew up writing my own poetry as a teen,” she said.

“There are definitely challenges that come with writing in the style. You can’t have paragraph-long descriptions, so the challenge is in distilling information down from maybe two paragraphs to one sentence.

“But I do love writing in that really spare and lyrical way. It just seems to come easily to me.

“I grew up loving song lyrics and music. I’m of the era where you pull the cover of the CDs and cassette tapes, and they’d have all the song lyrics printed on the covers.

“I’d be reading the song lyrics, and just absolutely loved it. So I think verse novels have that same sort of musicality as song lyrics.”

While Ms Bigna said the success of Little Bones has blown her away, she is already working on the release of her next book.

“There is something in the pipeline. The University of Queensland Press has acquired my next book,” she said.

“It’s not related to Little Bones, but it will also be written as a verse novel and will also be for the same readership age between nine and 12 years old.

“It will still explore deeper themes of friendship, healing and loss in a new, unique way that’s a bit different to Little Bones.

“There will be a bit of danger, a bit of adventure and a bit of exploration into change. I’m really looking forward to getting that into the hands of young readers around the middle of next year.”

Little Bones is available in paperback and hardcover through bookstores, or digitally on Kindle.

canberra.title: Are freight vehicles the ‘single biggest unclaimed opportunity left’ for ACT vehicles to be all-electric?
canberra.snippet: The ACT leads the country when it comes to new electric vehicle registrations but it’s received deductions for a lack of equal ince...
canberra.content:
The EV Council has ranked the ACT poorly when it comes to electrification of freight vehicles. Photo: James Coleman.

The ACT leads the country when it comes to new electric vehicle registrations but it’s received deductions for a lack of equal incentives for freight vehicles to join the movement.

The Territory scored high for several metrics measured in the latest EV Council 2026 report – receiving an overall score of 7/10.

The EV Council noted the Commonwealth, NSW and ACT were “performing at the top of the class” while South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Northern Territory had gone backwards.

“The reasons for this divergence are multifaceted, but two broad themes stand out: tighter fiscal conditions, which have limited all governments’ capacity to support the EV transition, and, in some jurisdictions, continued resistance to forward-looking transport policy in favour of ongoing reliance on fossil fuels,” it stated.

The number of electric vehicles being registered was a big plus in the ACT’s ranking.

Climate Change, Energy, Water and Waste Executive Group Manager Fiona Wright said 44 per cent of new cars being registered in Canberra were battery electric vehicles.

“If you add plug-in hybrids to that number, over half of the new vehicle registrations in the ACT were able to be plugged in [as of September],” Ms Wright said.

“That’s about double the national average.”

The number of ultra-fast DC connectors in the ACT also markedly grew, meaning there’s now one connector for every 206 battery-electric vehicles in the Territory (from 224).

But the ACT still lacks meaningful contribution to freight electrification.

The EV Council labelled freight trucks as the “single biggest unclaimed opportunity left” in the transport electrification space.

“Heavy vehicles are a small slice of the fleet, an out-sized slice of emissions and fuel imports,” the report stated.

An open letter to the Commonwealth signed by 46 freight industry leaders called on a national fuel strategy to cut costs for operators, reduce import dependence and to position Australia as a leader in “clean freight logistics”.

“This is not one voice asking for change. It is an entire industry — aligned, ready, and asking Australian governments to move with them,” the April letter stated.

“Without a step-change in policy, we risk being left behind by every major freight economy in the world.”

It also called on state and territory governments to grant electric trucks consistent road access, more incentives for all electric heavy-vehicle classes, and to reform curfews to enable overnight electric freight deliveries.

Heavier vehicles that are being targeted to go electric in the ACT include buses and garbage trucks. Photo: Transport Canberra.

The ACT received its lowest score in the freight vehicle category – 2/10.

By comparison, Victoria received 7/10, NSW 6/10 and the Commonwealth 5/10. All other jurisdictions received scores of one or zero.

“NSW and Victoria are the only jurisdictions making a meaningful contribution to freight electrification, while jurisdictions need to seriously consider the fuel insecurity they are imposing on their constituents by continuing to rely on petrol and diesel,” the report stated.

The ACT has endorsed a global push to speed up the adoption of zero-emission heavy vehicles, with a commitment to enable 100 per cent of zero-emission new truck sales by 2040.

But the EV Council noted the Territory doesn’t have a strategy to accelerate fleet turnover, has minimal available financial incentives and hasn’t made changes to allow for more electric heavy vehicle road access.

Light, heavy and articulated trucks account for about 1 per cent of registered vehicles in the ACT.

An ACT Government spokesperson said fast electric vehicle (DC) charging hubs presented a chance to better support this space.

“[Work is underway] to identify viable locations [for such hubs],” they said.

“These facilities would be able to support freight vehicles and other commercial vehicles that don’t have access to depot charging.”

They pointed out that, despite the ACT’s low score for incentives for fleets and businesses to go electric, there were options already available.

“ACT businesses have access to free advice on transitioning their vehicles to electric through the Fleet Advisory Service, as well as a rebate of up to $3300 for installing charging infrastructure,” the spokesperson said.

“A new action of the ACT Climate Change Strategy 2026-2036 will introduce zero emission vehicle expectations and transition planning for government contracts with significant transport components. This will also incentivise business fleets to transition their fleets to EVs.

“Transport is our highest source of emissions, and the new Climate Change Strategy acknowledges the need for behavioural change. We’ve also outlined that future action plans in the strategy will focus on additional measures to expand access to reliable, affordable and low-emissions transport.”

canberra.title: High Society Cafe at Torrens has the makings of a suburban gem
canberra.snippet: The gently curved amphitheatre of Torrens Shops makes it one of Canberra’s more retro-chic suburban shopping centres. It also makes...
canberra.content:
24 October 2026

Start the conversation

The cafe’s sunny exterior tempted many customers. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

The gently curved amphitheatre of Torrens Shops makes it one of Canberra’s more retro-chic suburban shopping centres. It also makes for a great people-watching location, especially from the outdoor dining area of High Society Cafe tucked into one edge of the curve.

The cafe opened in August and has clearly already become a favourite local haunt.

Friends caught up while their greyhound snoozed in the sun, students tapped away on laptops in the shade, and a group of teachers from the nearby school popped by on their lunch break. There’s plenty of space to sit inside, but most people can’t resist the space outside, either luxuriating (like the greyhound) in the sun or under the shade of the awning. A few potted plants soften the brick walls.

The all-day-brunch menu is comprehensive and creative.

I’m intrigued by the Nest Eggs – poached eggs in a ‘nest’ of angel-hair potato rosti with gochujang hollandaise – but ultimately can’t go past the folded chilli eggs.

The all-day-brunch menu turns out to be perfect for a mid-morning catch-up between someone who hasn’t had breakfast (me) and someone who’s been awake with kids since before 6 am and is ready for lunch (definitely not me).

My friend opts for the chicken burger: a classic!

Silky-soft chilli-folded eggs make a lovely breakfast dish. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

We’re focused on caffeine, so we order our usuals, but the drinks menu also offers smoothies and colourful specialty drinks like iced matcha or taro. I spy a few tables opting for iced drinks on this warm Spring morning.

The chilli eggs are carefully folded and stirred into a soft spiral, then served on two generous slices of seeded toast. I could have handled a little more heat in the chilli oil, but I enjoyed the crunch of fried shallots and sesame seeds.

Crispy sage leaves and soft pieces of goat’s curd scattered across the top add extra flavour, while the generous side of chorizo is tasty too.

The chicken burger disappears in record time, as do the chunky chips. Clearly a winner.

High Society Cafe’s menu features classic brunch dishes and a few unique offerings. Photo: High Society Cafe.

I’m keen to return another time for dishes like the chicken karaage rice bowl with edamame beans and furikake seasoning, or the indulgent pancake stack (which appears to be served with a full ice cream cone!)

It’s nice to see another section of these underrated local shops getting some love. And High Society Cafe has the makings of a proper suburban gem, one that will attract a regular crowd of locals and even tempt people from across town to visit.

High Society Cafe is located at Torrens Place, Torrens. They are open Monday to Friday from 6.30 am to 3 pm, and from 7 am to 3 pm on weekends. Follow High Society Cafe on Instagram.

canberra.title: Never heard of Kho Kho? Neither had half these Canberra players, until they gave it a go
canberra.snippet: Imagine a game of tag where you cannot simply turn around to chase someone. Instead, you must race around a pole or tap a teammate on the...
canberra.content:
Players chase and dodge opponents during the Kho Kho Independence Day Cup at Taylor 1 Sports Ground, where 24 participants took part in Canberra’s first formal competition of the traditional Indian sport. Photo: Supplied.

Imagine a game of tag where you cannot simply turn around to chase someone. Instead, you must race around a pole or tap a teammate on the back, shout “Kho!” and let them take over.

Welcome to Kho Kho, one of India’s oldest traditional sports, now attracting a new set of players in Canberra.

At Taylor 1 Sports Ground, 24 people aged between 12 and 40 gathered for what organisers believe was the ACT’s first formal Kho Kho competition.

The surprising part? More than half had never even heard of the game. Yet after a short introduction and a few practice matches, they were chasing, dodging and competing in a sport that demands speed, strategy and split-second decisions.

For generations of Indians, Kho Kho has been a familiar playground game. But in Australia, where cricket dominates much of the sporting connection with India, it remains largely unknown.

Federation of Indian Associations ACT (FINACT) president Sahithi Paturi wanted to change that.

“I saw Kho Kho as a wonderful opportunity to introduce a traditional Indian sport to Canberra, particularly because many people here have had little or no exposure to it,” she said.

The rules are unusual but relatively simple. Two teams take turns chasing and defending. Eight players from the chasing side sit in a line facing alternating directions, while a ninth pursues three defenders trying to avoid being tagged.

The chaser cannot freely reverse direction. Instead, they can run around a pole at either end of the court or tap a seated teammate and call “Kho!” to hand over the chase.

Each successful tag earns a point. The result is a rapid succession of sprints, sharp turns and tactical decisions, with players constantly switching between watching, waiting and chasing.

“Kho Kho requires speed, agility, teamwork, strategy and quick decision-making,” Ms Paturi said.

At the Canberra competition, the 24 participants were divided into Team A and Team B, with Team A emerging victorious. But the organisers were just as interested in how quickly newcomers took to the sport. “Many participants had never played Kho Kho before, but they were enthusiastic about learning and giving it a go,” Ms Paturi said.

“It was particularly rewarding to see how quickly they picked up the rules, encouraged one another and enjoyed the excitement of the game.”

Players from outside the Indian community also joined the competition, giving the event a broader cultural dimension.

Kho Kho had previously appeared in Canberra through exhibition matches, but FINACT says this was the first time the ACT had hosted a formal competition.

For Ms Paturi, the experience highlighted an opportunity to introduce Australians to sporting traditions beyond cricket. The challenge, she said, was not necessarily finding players or facilities. It was making people aware that the game existed.

“I think one of the biggest challenges is awareness. If people have never heard of a sport, they may not know how to get involved or where they can play it.”

The event attracted more than 30 spectators and community representatives, including ACT government minister and Member for Yerrabi Suzanne Orr, and shadow sport minister James Milligan.

Chinmay Suresh Pandit, First Secretary (Press, Information and Culture) at the High Commission of India in Canberra, also attended.

FINACT organised the competition in partnership with Kho Kho Canberra, with support from the High Commission of India.

Whether the sport will find a permanent place in Canberra remains an open question. Ms Paturi said there were no immediate plans for an annual competition or school program, with organisers intending to assess feedback before deciding what comes next.

But the first outing offered an encouraging sign. “Our experience showed that once people are introduced to Kho Kho and given an opportunity to practise, they can learn quickly and genuinely enjoy the game.”

Want to learn more? Visit Kho Kho Canberra.

canberra.title: Wet winter pushes back reopening date for Gibraltar Falls
canberra.snippet: Gibraltar Falls’ reopening date has been pushed back by several months as construction continues to make the site safer for everyon...
canberra.content:
24 October 2026

Join the conversation

2

Gibraltar Falls has remained inaccessible since two men fell to their deaths in separate incidents in 2023. Photo: ACT Government.

Gibraltar Falls’ reopening date has been pushed back by several months as construction continues to make the site safer for everyone.

Two young men fell to their deaths at the site in separate incidents in February 2023, and closure was initially flagged as a last resort.

An ACT spokesperson said this had been done out of an “abundance of caution” following the tragic deaths.

“Actions included closing the former carpark and access to the top of the falls, installing fencing and signage, and restricting access to high-risk areas,” they said.

A permanent 210-metre fence has since been erected along the Gibraltar Falls walking track, and the 2024–25 ACT Budget announced $3.68 million to deliver major upgrades and improve visitor facilities and access across the Woods Reserve and Gibraltar Falls precinct.

The Woods Reserve Campground closed in October 2025 as part of works to make it the new access point for the falls.

Works were meant to be completed by mid-2026, but delays have meant the campground and Gibraltar Falls are now not expected to open until early 2027.

“Works have been delayed by wet winter conditions, which affected site access and construction activities,” the ACT Government spokesperson said.

“The extended closure is not solely related to the installation of safety infrastructure. Additional time is required to complete final works, landscaping and site establishment so the precinct is ready to safely reopen to the public.”

While it’s hoped the area will re-open in early 2027, that is subject to completion of the remaining works and site readiness to start receiving visitors again.

The major works on a walking track to connect the campground with Snake Rock, near Gibraltar Falls, are complete, but final landscaping, site establishment and other finishing touches still need to be ticked off.

The ACT Government spokesperson said the works were about making the precinct both safer and more accessible for everyone to enjoy.

“The redevelopment provides longer-term improvements to safety, access and visitor facilities across the broader Woods Reserve and Gibraltar Falls precinct, including upgraded trails, viewing areas, signage, visitor amenities and redesigned access arrangements,” they said.

“We know many Canberrans are looking forward to returning to the Woods Reserve and Gibraltar Falls area, and we appreciate the community’s patience while the works are completed.

“While the precinct remains closed, Canberrans and visitors can continue to enjoy other campgrounds and walking trails across ACT parks and reserves.”

australia.title: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public
australia.snippet: WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’ Get our new political email...
australia.content:
Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator apologises for publicly releasing the letter outlining the claims against him.

On Saturday afternoon, Steele-John removed a social media post containing a three-page letter marked as “confidential” sent to the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, earlier this month. The letter urged an investigation into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.

Steele-John has denied all allegations made against him.

The Western Australian senator said he’d heard the full letter had been circulating online and “didn’t want to be seen as hiding from it”.

“I’m now not sure that was the right call and I’ve taken it down. I am really sorry for any additional stress it caused,” he said on social media.

After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, the now-deleted statement posted to social media late Friday night said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”.

He would instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.

Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” were made had now been set.

“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with Shoebridge over whether he was on leave during the investigation.

The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.

The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear of backlash. The letter provided no further detail.

In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025. Steele-John later responded this was alleged by a former partner and was investigated by Western Australian police with a finding of “no charges”.

Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch of releasing the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.

australia.title: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack
australia.snippet: Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital Get our breaking news email , free app or dai...
australia.content:
Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.

The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.

“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.

The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”

“I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.

“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.

Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.

On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday.

“What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”

Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered.

“We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read.

The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debat, security risks for MPs and mental health services in regional Victoria.

WA Police charged a 56-year-old man after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines.

A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.

Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.

australia.title: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia
australia.snippet: Parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by Sunday Get our br...
australia.content:
Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.

Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.

The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.

Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.

“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.

The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.

“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.

This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.

“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.

The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.

“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.

On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.

Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.

The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

australia.title: Complex issues: how to get your apartment block off gas – before it’s too late
australia.snippet: Electrifying your block of flats could cut emissions and save money. Don’t wait to plan the change Change by degrees offers life hacks an...
australia.content:
Around Australia, homes are getting off gas. Gas cooktops are being swapped for induction stoves, gas hot water replaced by heat pumps, and gas space heating with reverse cycle air conditioners.

In combination with solar panels, batteries and better insulation, electrification saves money, cuts emissions and makes homes healthier to live in.

Electrifying a freestanding house is often straightforward. Apartments are more challenging because you generally need your neighbours’ cooperation.

Complex issues

“It’s relatively easy for an individual apartment owner to replace a gas cooktop with an induction stove,” says Luke Barry, an engineer at GHD.

But if every apartment owner in a building does the same thing, he warns, then the extra electrical load could overwhelm the main switchboard.

Piecemeal replacement of gas appliances with electric devices and uncoordinated installation of electrical vehicle chargers may even require an expensive upgrade of the building’s connection to the grid.

Extra load can be offset by installing solar panels, and it’s now possible to fairly distribute the power they generate with technology like SolShare, which won top honours in the 2026 Australian Good Design Awards.

But many apartments also have centralised gas-fired facilities like hot water heaters, swimming pool heaters, or HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) systems that provide building-wide heating, ventilation and cooling and rely on gas boilers to generate warmth.

  • Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

Replacing this equipment requires action by the organisation that manages common property in a building, known in some states as the owners corporation and in others as the strata corporation or body corporate.

“Usually in energy efficiency you are dealing either with owner-occupiers or with tenants and their landlords,” says Trent Jones, founder and managing director of All Electric Homes. “But in an apartment complex you also have a third actor to contend with – the owners corporation and its elected committee.”

While all apartment owners are automatic members of the owners corporation, many pay little attention to committee meetings and decisions, making it hard to get everyone on board with big changes like electrification.

Sometimes, everything goes smoothly. At the recent High Life Living expo, Jones presented a case study of a block of 18 flats in Brunswick in Melbourne’s inner north. The owners contracted All Electric Homes to replace their building’s failing gas hot water system with a bank of heat pumps backed by solar panels. The work took four days and wiped out the building’s $19,000 annual gas bill. The investment paid for itself in less than two years.

In a larger apartment building, the issues can be more complex.

It’s technically difficult, for example, to replace the gas boilers in HVAC systems with heat pumps. First, the boilers need to generate much higher temperatures than can easily be achieved with heat pumps. Second, it can be hard to find enough room for banks of heat pumps, especially in towers that have lots of apartments and limited roof space.

As GHD’s senior sustainability consultant, Barry is leading a City of Melbourne program to assess the feasibility of electrifying 13 medium- and high-rise apartment buildings. He hopes that these case studies will chart new ways forward for retrofitting existing apartment blocks.

Plan ahead

The problems are not just technical.

“The technical solutions are often quite easy,” says Jones. “The difficulty is getting everyone to agree on what needs to be done.”

“The larger the building, the more likely it is that there’ll be dissent,” says Dr Janette Corcoran, board director of the not-for-profit Owners Corporation Network that advocates for people who own and live in strata titled apartments.

Presenting electrification as an environmental initiative can complicate the issue by polarising neighbours into pro- and anti-groups, she cautions.

“Lowering emissions appeals to some people but not to everyone. Once people feel you’ve got an agenda, they start getting their backs up.”

To defuse this risk, Corcoran recommends treating electrification like any other major work to maintain a property in good condition.

“There are always a lot of infrastructure needs to be looked at in an apartment building. For example, a lot of buildings may need facade replacement or lift upgrades.”

She recommends that owners committees include the replacement of gas equipment in their plans for long-term maintenance and capital works.

With a horizon of a decade or so, these plans don’t just consider what upgrades are needed and when, but also enable owners to smooth costs by gradually accumulating funds to pay for major works without blowing the budget.

This reduces the risk of being caught out when gas equipment fails and the owners corporation is forced into emergency mode to replace it quickly.

“People hate special levies,” Corcoran says, referring to extra charges when apartment owners must cough up for sudden unforeseen expenses. “If you have a plan and the plan is approved by the owners, then you can act in a planned and sequenced manner.”

As a first step, she recommends a holistic energy audit to determine how much energy a building consumes, for what purposes, from what sources and at what times.

“There are many moving parts, and the best approach is to have rock solid information.”

It’s imperative for all residential buildings to get off gas over the next two-and-a-half decades for Australia to achieve net zero by 2050.

“If you are looking to rent or buy an apartment, consider an apartment that is already electrified or can be electrified relatively easily,” Corcoran suggests.

She urges residents in existing apartments to start “tilling the soil” for electrification by asking their owners corporation committee how they are preparing to replace gas assets before they age out.

While electrification can be complex, kicking the can down the road poses huge financial risks. As fewer households use gas, those remaining on the network will face escalating bills as they carry a bigger share of network costs. Apartment residents still reliant on gas in the 2030s and 2040s could find themselves stuck with an expensive, stranded asset.

“You don’t want to be left holding the baby,” says Corcoran. “You’ve got to have a plan, you’ve got to have a strategy, and they’ve got to be approved.”

australia.title: Jordon Steele-John’s position remains in limbo as Greens prepare for moment in spotlight
australia.snippet: David Shoebridge’s newly-minted leadership under pressure over handling of misconduct allegations as Senate estimates looms Get our new p...
australia.content:
More than a week after allegations that Greens senator Jordon Steele-John had behaved inappropriately towards women made headlines, his position in the party remains in limbo and its new leader’s handling of the issue in question.

David Shoebridge’s first major challenge at the helm of the federal Greens came earlier this month when the Nine newspapers reported a three-page letter had been sent to him urging an independent investigation into Steele-John.

It referred to secondhand allegations that the Western Australian senator had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.

As a progressive party that prides itself on taking such matters seriously and fairly, it made sense that Shoebridge announced the 32-year-old’s leave amid an independent probe into the claims.

But the process quickly became more complicated. Days later, a defiant Steele-John rejected the allegations against him, denied he agreed to take leave from parliament, and accused an internal faction within the WA Greens of playing “nasty political games” in its decision to release the letter to the media.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Steele-John said he made a public statement because he didn’t want his silence on the letter’s claims to be perceived as guilt.

While Shoebridge insists Steele-John agreed to take leave, he acknowledges he alone does not have the power to force the senator to do so.

Only if two-thirds of the party room – or more than seven members – decided to expel him in a secret ballot would Steele-John have to comply.

Such a move would be nuclear. Even if the WA Greens’ independent investigation clears him of any wrongdoing, Steele-John’s standing in the party room would be shattered.

The week ahead under scrutiny

Senate estimates is a time for members of the upper house to have their moment in the spotlight. For the Greens, it’s a chance to extricate answers about government policies from carefully trained bureaucrats to drive home a political point.

With the NDIS undergoing major changes between now and the decade’s end, Steele-John, who is championed and well-liked within the disability community as the party’s disability spokesperson, will not attend.

Steele-John issued a statement late Friday saying he had explored attending digitally, but had “been informed that would also be unacceptable”.

“As such I have decided not to return next week and will instead focus on the independent and timely investigation I hope is soon commenced by the Greens WA,” Steele-John said.

For many supporters within and outside the Greens, the optics of allowing a federal party member accused of sexual misconduct – even though a complainant has not directly come forward to make those allegations – to continue public duties would have been a tough pill to swallow. Particularly as the “manosphere” phenomenon and backlash against the #MeToo movement gain momentum in mainstream society.

The question over whether the allegations were politically motivated by adversaries of Steele-John looking to gain advantage in the state’s pre-selection is a part of the equation.

But the fact remains that the rumours have persisted over the senator’s time in office. Even if they are malicious, as Steele-John contends, the simpler option would still be to stand aside and settle them while they are investigated.

The decision over whether to force Steele-John to take leave will be as much about Shoebridge’s leadership as it is about the party’s processes.

The party room, and its membership more broadly, prides itself on being a movement based on consensus decision-making.

Shoebridge will need the support of the party room to take the expulsion route. How he handles this issue will also set the tone for the rest of his leadership and, depending on his actions, could prompt an ugly battle with Steele-John.

It’s a quagmire – politically, legally and ethically.

There are unlikely to be any winners.

world.title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
world.snippet: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials acro...
world.content:
Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.

The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.

“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
world.snippet: 41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’ Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record Lewis Hamilton has said h...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

world.title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
world.snippet: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’ The US-backed hepat...
world.content:
The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.

Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

world.title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
world.snippet: Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail Send us your questions ...
world.content:
Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday-night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, in a statement to the Guardian late on Wednesday, said it was “a false story designed to smear the brave men and women of ICE as they are facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them”.

“No sick detainees are being deported. All detainees are medically cleared before travel and leave with any necessary medications.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said her husband has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.

Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.

“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

The DHS statement said Sendra was “a criminal illegal alien from Cuba convicted of fraud, larceny, and property crimes” and “has been consistently cleared and discharged from the hospital following medical evaluation”.

He was ordered removed from the US in September 2015, it said.

“Third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets,” the spokesperson said.

“Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal, and the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe.”

Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.

The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

world.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
world.snippet: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its c...
world.content:
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.
